en: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Praise of the Discourses:
The teaching of the Dhamma is penetrating.
I pay homage to the King of Dharma,
who teaches the Dhamma of the world—
profound in four ways and difficult to see.
To the Buddha, the Paccekabuddha,
the Arahant, and the Cakkavatti—
I pay homage to those who are worthy of stupas and those who are not.
Among those worthy of a fourth-tier stupa,
he was one who slept like a petta and enjoyed sensual pleasures;
the Tathāgata, however, sleeps in the lion’s posture.
Reclining on the four postures,
the Conqueror is known by the fourth name;
those born from eggs and those born from a womb.
Moisture-born and spontaneously born;
the classification of the four modes of birth—
I bow to the Victor, the possessor of knowledge.
The Buddha of Scripture, the Buddha who has awakened after others, the Solitary Buddha, and the Fully Enlightened Buddha— these are the four Buddhas,
with the fourth being among the four types of Buddhas.
I pay homage to the Leader of the World;
Rāhu is the foremost among those with bodies,
and Mandhātā is the foremost among those who enjoy sensual pleasures.
Māra is the foremost among those who exercise sovereignty,
and the Buddha is the foremost in the world including the devas,
among those things established as the fourfold excellence.
I bow to the Jina who has reached the pinnacle.
Generosity, pleasant speech,
purposeful conduct, and impartiality;
To the one who gathers the world through the four bases of sympathy throughout incalculable births.
I pay homage to the Leader of the World;
greed, hatred, and delusion—
these three are the internal enemies.
Even one who is well-restrained and wise should bow before those difficult for all enemies to conquer,
due to the greatness of their birth and merit.
Possessing the supreme greatness of virtues and endowed with the three great powers,
I pay homage to the Leader of the World.
Endowed with the perfection of cause and fruit,
and the perfection of service to beings—
endowed with these three perfections.
I pay homage to the Leader of the World,
who possesses the power of wisdom and abandonment,
and the perfection of a beautiful form.
I bow to that Jina who is perfected through the fourfold accomplishments:
perfection of aspiration and perfection of application.
The perfection of assistance to beings;
may that Victor, in whom these two are perfected, protect me rightly.
To Mahosadha, to Vessantara,
and likewise to one in their final existence—
one should bow with speech before these three types of persons.
While he was speaking at the moment of his birth,
and concerning Nemi Sādhina,
Mandhātā, and Guttila.
I pay homage to him who, having been a human being among the four [classes],
has gone to the world of the gods.
Conditioned phenomena are transformations of form.
Characteristic, the unconditioned,
Nibbāna, and conceptualization—
these five knowable objects I revere.
The renunciation of son and wife,
the renunciation of a portion of the kingdom, and the renunciation of life—
these are the five great renunciations.
I pay homage to him who performs what is most difficult to do:
form, feeling, perception,
mental formations, and consciousness— these are the last.
One who fully understands the five aggregates through the three types of full knowledge—
those humans and gods, I bow to them.
Peta, Niraya, and likewise Tiracchāna—
these five destinies I bow to as they cut [through] me.
The son of a deva, the defilement,
the Māra of volitional formations,
and the aggregates— these five are called death.
One should pay homage to the Conqueror of Māra—
at morning, at afternoon,
and likewise at the first and middle watches of the night.
I bow to him who always performs the five final duties of a Buddha:
forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and...
And delightful tangibles—
having abandoned these five strands of sensual pleasure as if they were spittle fallen from the mouth, one should pay homage [to the Buddha].
The arrow of passion, the arrow of hatred,
and delusion, conceit, and views—
I pay homage to him who has transcended these faults.
The Removal of the Five Arrows.
The Long, the Middle, the Saṃyutta,
the Aṅguttara, and the Khuddaka.
Thus, with these five Nikāyas,
one should revere the people who are well-disciplined;
sovereignty, fame, and the Dhamma—
Desire, glory, and diligence—
endowed with these six fortunes,
I revere the Leader of the World.
Whether pleasant or unpleasant, true or untrue,
beneficial or harmful as appropriate—
mixed with these six, one should speak well-spoken words.
One should honor one who speaks for the sake of the goal.
Laziness, negligence,
lack of exertion, and lack of restraint—
One should always bow to the six openings with the cord of sleep;
this is the attainment of great compassion.
The Twin Miracle; knowledge of the underlying tendencies in their latent state;
and the higher and lower degrees of the faculties.
I bow to the six unshared qualities of the Omniscient One: omniscience, absence of obstruction, and the [three knowledges],
as well as freedom from sensual desire and ill will.
Lethargy and drowsiness, doubt,
ignorance, restlessness, and remorse—
I bow to this sixfold hindrance.
The modes of supernormal power, the divine ear,
the knowledge of others' minds,
and the recollection of past lives.
With the divine eye and the destruction of the taints,
endowed with the six direct knowledges—
I pay homage to that Supreme Person.
Blue, yellow, and white,
madder-red and brilliant, and crimson—
thus by six rays, they shine.
I always pay homage to that which shines brightly:
its gratification, its danger,
and likewise its escape and fruit.
I bow to the teacher of the true Dhamma, who possesses the sixfold command of skillful means:
lust, hatred, and delusion—
Likewise, the modes of thought;
those six modes of conduct, which distribute faith and wisdom, I revere.
Silver, gold, pearls,
gems, beryl, and diamonds, as well as coral—
Like the merchant Sattadhanu:
faith, virtue, learning, and generosity;
shame and fear of wrongdoing are his wealth.
I pay homage to the Fully Awakened One, the possessor of the seven great treasures, who has wisdom as his wealth. [The seven treasures are:
the wheel, the elephant, the horse, the jewel, ...
Likewise, the householders’ wives,
the excellent leader,
and the wheel-turning monarch with seven treasures.
Mindfulness and investigation of phenomena,
as well as energy and rapture;
tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.
I pay homage to the Supreme Person, the turner of the wheel of the true Dhamma, who possesses the jewel of the seven factors of enlightenment.
Yugandhara, Īṣādhara,
Karavīka, Sudassana;
Nemindhara, Vinataka.
And Assakaṇṇa on the Great Mountain—
bowing to the Victor who beholds these seven as if they were the form of an elephant.
Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Anotatta,
Kuṇāla, Rathakāraka;
Sīhappapāta, Chaddanta.
And the great lake Mandākinī—
seeing all these seven in every way,
one should bow down even upon seeing them.
Human birth, possession of the [right] gender,
The cause, seeing the Teacher,
Going forth, and perfection of virtues.
Authority and zeal—
through the combination of these eight factors,
one should pay homage to the one who carries out the schism.
It was distinct, charming, and intelligible,
delightful to hear and not straying;
its deep resonance fell like a falling drop.
I pay homage to the essence of the Eightfold Path.
Likewise, there are the four fine-material jhānas and the immaterial jhānas.
Those attainments are eight;
one who practices them according to one's preference will incline [toward success].
The powers of atomization, levitation, and action—
Majesty, glory, as well as lordship,
mastery, and the power to dispose of things according to one's will.
Because he possesses the perfection of the eight masteries,
I pay homage to Issarātissa, who possesses the supernormal power of the mind-made body and the knowledge of supernormal powers.
I pay homage to the ornament of the three worlds, endowed with the six direct knowledges, insight,
and the eight types of knowledge.
Birth, aging, illness, death,
and the suffering of the four states of misery—
these are the eight grounds for spiritual urgency.
I pay homage to the one who speaks in various ways:
the discourses (sutta), the analytical expositions (veyyākaraṇa),
the mixed prose and verse (geyya), the verses (gāthā), and the birth stories (jātaka).
The Marvels, the Question-and-Answer texts,
the Inspired Utterances, and the Itivuttakas—
this is the ninefold division for all the world.
I pay homage to the Teaching that bestows gifts.
Those eight attainments together with cessation— these are nine.
One should bow to one who,
by choice, cultivates those successive dwellings—
both unity and diversity.
Through association with those possessing perception of the body, there are four; likewise the formless [attainments];
and the non-percipient—these are nine.
I bow to the Victor who, having analyzed the seven abodes, reveals them;
he who is equal to the superior and even superior to the superior.
"Inferior" is of three kinds;
likewise for the similar and the inferior;
one should bow to those who dispel these nine kinds.
He acts for my harm,
he has acted so, and he will act;
a friend does not act for the enemy's harm.
I bow down to the one who has abandoned the nine kinds of resentment:
generosity, virtue, renunciation,
wisdom, and energy as the fifth.
Having fulfilled the perfections— patience, the resolve for truth,
loving-kindness, and equanimity—
I pay homage to the Neutral One (Tāda).
The horse Sammāsambodhi, Majjhava, Kāḷāvaka, Gaṅgeyya,
Paṇḍara, Tamba, and Piṅgala.
Gandhamaṅgalahemaca, Uposathachaddantime;
He who observes these ten Uposatha days,
[attains great merit].
The elephant Kāḷāvaka is powerful;
he is the peerless Chaddanta,
who feeds a thousand crores of followers.
The strength of ten thousand koṭis of elephants that carry burdens,
and that of ten six-tusked elephants—
I pay homage to the One with Ten Powers:
who knows what is possible and impossible, the ripening of kamma,
and the path that leads everywhere.
Knowledge of the various elements in the world,
of the inclinations of living beings,
and of their individual differences.
Knowledge regarding the faculties and living beings,
prior knowledge of jhānas and so forth,
recollection of past lives, and the divine eye.
The knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsava-kkhaya-ñāṇa) is named the knowledge of the Ten Powers (dasabala-ñāṇa). [It is like] the root,
the fragrance, the heartwood, and the sapwood.
Taco, papaṭika, and rasa;
patta, puppha, and phala;
and gandha-gandha—this is the restraint.
I always bow to him who anoints himself with ten kinds of fragrant scents;
through the expansion of concentration and knowledge, he is ever radiant.
Resolution, transformation,
the mind-made, and noble psychic power,
as well as that born of the ripening of kamma.
The power of knowledge belongs to the meritorious;
the power of effort is the supernormal power of conditions;
[this is] the foremost among the ten powers.
I bow to him who performs miracles:
pearl, gem, beryl,
conch shell, coral, and ruby.
Gold, silver, ruby, emerald,
and cat’s-eye— by these ten gems, the earth is adorned.
I pay homage to the Serpent with the jewel of wisdom.
[He who knows] the lax and the firm, the long and the short,
the heavy and the light;
I bow to the Dhamma which reveals the elided vowel, the released, the connected, the established, and the expanded.
It is distinguished by ten qualities: serenity, vigor, sweetness,
evenness, and delicacy;
Syllabic clarity, majesty, beauty,
lucidity of meaning, and composure— endowed with these ten qualities of speech, [the Buddha’s word is sublime].
I pay homage to him who protects the Dhamma.
Greed, hatred, delusion, conceit,
restlessness, wrong view, and doubt—
Lack of shame, lack of dread, and sloth—
these ten defilements together are all-burning.
I bow to Vāsanāyaja.
Saterā, Daṇḍamaṇikā,
and Macchavilolagaggarā.
The dried bones, the monkey-heads,
the cross-roads, the perception, and the cocks;
with these nine seats, he plows.
One should pay homage to the one possessing sharp wisdom.
Likewise, there are weeping, the weapon of anger, and the casting away of sovereignty.
I pay homage to that reflection and patience among the eight powers, which is like the earth.
With the eighth, the Guide:
sensual desire as a disease, aversion,
conceit, views, and doubt.
I bow to those who have overcome latent tendencies toward existence— namely, Bhavarāga and Avijjā— as well as to the heretics,
the ordinary disciples, and the great disciples.
The chief disciples, the paccekabuddhas, and the fully enlightened Buddhas—
those who know their former abodes— are preeminent in all six ways.
I pay homage to the Crown of the Three Worlds. To the Buddha-eye,
the universal wisdom, and the divine eye;
I have seen the Dhamma with five eyes;
I bow to the Conqueror of Māra.
The minor, the momentary, and the intrusive [fear].
Pharaṇā and likewise ubbegā—
those five who fill [beings] with the jhāna-factors of joy,
I bow to them with devotion.
Suffering, the truth of its origin,
cessation, and the truth of the path—
by fully understanding these four truths, [one attains liberation].
One should pay homage to those who perform the four duties:
oppression, the meaning of the conditioned,
austerity, and transformation.
I pay homage to the Sage who analyzed the truth of suffering through fourfold sets:
accumulation and its source, and so forth.
I bow to the Sage who has analyzed the origin [of suffering] through the fourfold sets, and who has explained that conjunction is an obstacle.
Escape and seclusion,
as well as the unconditioned and the Deathless;
and cessation— by means of these tetrads.
I pay homage to the Sage who has analyzed [the Dhamma]:
the purpose of the cause is leading out,
and its sovereignty is through vision.
I pay homage to the Sage who analyzed the Truth of the Path through fourfold sets: the Teacher,
Non-delusion, and so forth.
Having a suitable range of resort,
and devoid of the fourfold lack of clear comprehension—
I bow to the Tathāgata who has developed these qualities.
I pay homage to him who has abandoned all suffering,
who has reached the further shore of the ocean of existence,
and who is endowed with essential virtues.
By that, I have gone beyond existence.
It is connected with the supreme splendor of form and formlessness, and with inconceivable forms.
I pay homage to him who is endowed with essential virtues;
therefore, I am one of incomparable beauty.
O you whose supernatural power is the pinnacle of majestic splendor!
I shall contemplate the power (iddhi) associated with this;
I praise him who possesses the quality of essence,
for that reason we are called those possessing incomparable power.
I pay homage to the supreme play of speech,
to the speech that is well-composed and endowed with the quality of essence.
Therefore, I am a speaker of measured words.
O pinnacle of the play of knowledge,
O you who are conjoined with inconceivable wisdom!
I pay homage to him who is endowed with essential qualities;
therefore, we say he possesses incomparable knowledge.
Silver, gold, and jewels—these are [mere] surface-decorations.
A house, clothing, and food—
whatever else [is desired] according to my heart's wish—
I shall provide; I bow to the Jina.
Gold, jewels, a house, clothing, and food—
whatever else there may be according to one's heart's desire—
I would build it through the supernormal power born of karma.
The Sage, a jewel of the seven factors of enlightenment, possesses the jewels of faith and the rest.
I pay homage to that Supreme Person, the Jewel beginning with Mindfulness,
possessing the seven jewels such as the Wheel.
I obtained the beautiful jewels such as pearls,
and the jewels such as fine cloth,
at the moment of my resolve.
One whose heart's intention is fulfilled,
who attains whatever he desires,
and who is not overcome by anyone—
I pay homage to the Conqueror named Sabbābhibhū,
whose thoughts and intentions are fulfilled,
who attains exactly what he desires.
He who is unconquered by anyone,
the Conqueror of All, in every state of existence—
just like the ten kings of the six inner continents.
The Sage possesses tenfold bodily power;
equal to him in tenfold power of knowledge,
I pay homage to that supreme ascetic.
The Buddha’s speed of body surpasses that of the royal swan;
what need is there to mention the speed of his knowledge?
I pay homage to that supreme ascetic, who,
like the elephant king Chaddanta,
is possessed of great strength in birth after birth.
Like a royal thoroughbred horse,
he shall possess supreme speed;
and like a water-fowl moving through the air.
The Conqueror who does not sink into the great flood,
the Maker who fashioned the mind according to its nature—
I pay homage to him who has reached the further shore of all that is to be known.
One who moves through the water by means of coughing,
one who sinks into the earth,
and a builder according to his own whim—
Through the power of karma,
one exists everywhere— in villages and forests—
among both gods and humans.
To that Great Seer who has always attained the pinnacle of gain in the world,
for whom infinite gains are brought forth—
I pay homage to that bull among sages,
who is everywhere— in villages and forests alike—
surrounded by gods and humans.
May infinite gain be brought to me,
always, in birth after birth;
by the power of this merit, may it be so.
May my mind be fulfilled;
may all my desires and all my thoughts quickly come to pass for one born again and again.
The word "there is not" is suffering,
and likewise the word "give";
therefore, [avoid] "there is not" and "give."
May there be no more for me in existence after existence.
All that is under the power of another is suffering;
all sovereignty is happiness.
Everything would be subject to another's power;
everything would become sovereign.
While he was thus reflecting, his body began to break apart.
May I, at the third birth, be one who wards off all weapons and possesses the strength of a six-tusked elephant.
Endowed with auspicious marks,
he shall be of golden complexion;
his voice like that of Brahmā, like the song of the karavīka bird.
And he who possesses vast wisdom regarding the various arts would become skilled in all of them.
He alone is capable of answering all questions on the spot;
and as for the wealth of Veradhamma, it too—
Possessing endless and inexhaustible wealth,
with an infinite assembly of followers,
he shall attain the auspicious state beyond existence.
May I not perish, may I not be overcome,
even by those striving together with me—
by the five hundred million who bear enmity toward me.
Or a vessel not intended for trade;
a cloud, wind, and a jewel;
grain, clothing, and food.
By the power of my supernormal knowledge born of karma,
may I create whatever else is desired;
through this merit, may there be Nibbāna.
By that much I attain peace;
may I always possess the fourfold excellence throughout all my births.
Endowed with the four wheels and the seven true qualities,
he is possessed of right view and wealth.
In a family esteemed as the best,
universally honored and utterly pure,
he was conceived through the conjunction of three causes.
One should not even with one's hand take grass, a roof-covering, or enjoyments; rather,
one should use them only through supernormal power (iddhi).
Having prepared as much food as desired,
surpassing that of humans,
like the food of the devas.
May I have clothing and wealth,
and a retinue most beautiful;
may even a fringe of my garment be a source of enjoyment.
The five enmities may arise from birth to birth;
they might seize one or cause one’s destruction, yet for the sake of wealth,
one remains free from sorrow.
Endowed with beauty in every limb,
with a complexion like refined gold,
and possessed of the thirty-two marks.
There may be a body that is not subject to affliction,
with the fragrance of sandalwood and a mouth with the scent of a blue lotus.
May I have an eightfold voice like that of the karavīka bird and the mañjūghosa;
may I possess sharp and profound wisdom.
Possessing laughter, extreme speed,
and wisdom, he is of vast and penetrative insight,
the resolver of all questions.
Before reaching the age of sixteen,
he became a master of the Tipiṭaka,
proficient in all ritual acts and crafts.
One who has reached the further shore of the fields of knowledge.
